items.question: Customers praised the _____ of the support staff after the system outage.
items.explanation: The blank needs a noun after "the." "Professionalism" is the noun that names the quality.
items.commonMistake: "Professional" is an adjective and cannot follow "the" as the object of praised.
items.learningObjective: After the + of, look for a noun naming a quality or action.

items.question: Ms. Alvarez prepared a _____ summary of last quarter's retail performance.
items.explanation: A word before a noun is usually an adjective. "Decisive" modifies "summary."
items.commonMistake: "Decisively" is an adverb and does not sit before a noun. "Decision" is a noun.
items.learningObjective: Place an adjective immediately before the noun it describes.

items.question: The consultant answered the board's questions _____ and without notes.
items.explanation: The blank modifies the verb "answered," so the adverb "clearly" is required.
items.commonMistake: "Clear" is an adjective. "Clarity" and "clearance" are nouns with different meanings.
items.learningObjective: Ask whether the blank describes an action (adverb) or a thing (adjective/noun).

items.question: Human Resources will _____ the new onboarding schedule next Monday.
items.explanation: After the modal "will," use the base verb: will announce.
items.commonMistake: Noun or -ing forms cannot follow will. "Announced" is past, not a base form.
items.learningObjective: Modal + base verb is a fixed pattern.

items.question: Mr. Kim _____ to Singapore last Tuesday for the supplier audit.
items.explanation: "Last Tuesday" is a finished past time, so the simple past "flew" is correct.
items.commonMistake: Present perfect ("has flown") is not used with a finished past date.
items.learningObjective: A specific past time cue means simple past.

items.question: The IT department _____ the email servers during this weekend's maintenance window.
items.explanation: The maintenance is in the future (this weekend), so "will upgrade" is the match.
items.commonMistake: Bare "upgrade" needs a subject-verb helper. "Upgraded" is past.
items.learningObjective: Use will + base verb for scheduled future work.

items.question: When the fire alarm sounded, the accounting team _____ the monthly close.
items.explanation: A longer action was in progress when a shorter past event interrupted it. Past continuous fits.
items.commonMistake: Simple present or present perfect do not describe a past-in-progress scene.
items.learningObjective: When + past event, past continuous for the background action.

items.question: The shuttle to the airport _____ every hour from the main lobby.
items.explanation: Timetables and regular schedules take present simple: "departs."
items.commonMistake: "Depart" does not agree with the singular subject "shuttle."
items.learningObjective: Use present simple for transport schedules and routines.

items.question: Ms. Patel is responsible _____ coordinating the intern orientation in June.
items.explanation: The collocation is "responsible for" + noun/gerund.
items.commonMistake: "Responsible of" is a common transfer error from other languages.
items.learningObjective: Learn adjective + preposition pairs as chunks.

items.question: Expense reports must be filed _____ the last business day of each month.
items.explanation: "By" means "no later than" a deadline. Filing should be complete on or before that day.
items.commonMistake: "Until" describes a continuing state, not a completion deadline. "During" needs a period, not a single day as a cutoff.
items.learningObjective: Use by for the latest acceptable time to finish something.

items.question: Several retailers have expressed interest _____ carrying our autumn catalog.
items.explanation: The phrase is "interest in" + gerund/noun.
items.commonMistake: "Interest on" is used for money (interest on a loan), not for liking something.
items.learningObjective: Remember interest in, not interest on, for topics and activities.

items.question: _____ the projector failed, the presenter continued using printed handouts.
items.explanation: "Although" introduces a full clause (subject + verb). "The projector failed" is a clause.
items.commonMistake: "Despite" and "because of" need a noun phrase, not a full sentence. "However" cannot start this pattern without punctuation changes.
items.learningObjective: Although/while/because + clause; despite/because of + noun.

items.question: The help desk extended its hours; _____, it added a weekend chat option.
items.explanation: The second idea is extra, not a replacement. "In addition" marks adding information.
items.commonMistake: "Instead" would mean the chat replaced the hours, which is not the meaning.
items.learningObjective: Use in addition / moreover for extra facts, not contrast.

items.question: The reservation will be canceled _____ we confirm it by 5:00 p.m.
items.explanation: "Unless" means "if not." The booking stays only if confirmation happens.
items.commonMistake: "If we confirm" would reverse the logic: confirmation would cause cancellation.
items.learningObjective: Unless = if not. Check whether the result happens without the action.

items.question: The supervisor _____ approved the overtime request is out of the office today.
items.explanation: The relative pronoun is the subject of "approved," so "who" is correct.
items.commonMistake: "Whom" is for objects. If you can replace it with he/she, use who.
items.learningObjective: Who = subject; whom = object; whose = possessive.

items.question: Team leads should complete the safety checklist _____ before the inspection.
items.explanation: "Team leads" is plural, so the reflexive is "themselves."
items.commonMistake: Himself/herself are singular and do not match a plural subject.
items.learningObjective: Match reflexive pronouns to the number of the subject.

items.question: Please forward _____ invoices that still lack a purchase-order number.
items.explanation: A demonstrative adjective is needed before the noun "invoices." "Those" fits.
items.commonMistake: "Them" is an object pronoun and cannot sit before a noun. "They" is a subject pronoun.
items.learningObjective: Use this/that/these/those before a noun; use them after a verb.

items.question: The warehouse manager, along with two clerks, _____ preparing the inventory count.
items.explanation: Phrases like "along with" do not change the subject. The subject is "manager" (singular): "is."
items.commonMistake: Learners agree with "clerks" because it is closer. Cover the middle phrase and re-read.
items.learningObjective: Along with / together with / as well as do not make a singular subject plural.

items.question: Neither the brochure nor the price list _____ the new warranty terms.
items.explanation: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. "Price list" is singular, so "mentions."
items.commonMistake: People choose a plural verb because two things are named. Agreement follows the nearest noun.
items.learningObjective: Neither A nor B → verb matches B.

items.question: A number of employees _____ volunteered for Saturday's community fair.
items.explanation: "A number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb: have volunteered.
items.commonMistake: "The number of" is singular. Do not mix the two patterns.
items.learningObjective: A number of + plural noun + plural verb.

items.question: If we _____ a larger warehouse, we could keep more stock on site.
items.explanation: An unreal present situation uses if + past, then would/could + base verb.
items.commonMistake: "If we have" is first conditional (real). "Would have" does not belong in the if-clause.
items.learningObjective: Second conditional: if + past, would/could + verb.

items.question: If the flight had been canceled, the team _____ the meeting by video.
items.explanation: A past unreal condition (had been canceled) pairs with would have + past participle.
items.commonMistake: "Would join" is second conditional (present unreal), not a finished past event.
items.learningObjective: Third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + past participle.

items.question: If customers _____ a damaged item, they should photograph the package immediately.
items.explanation: A standing rule uses if + present simple. "Receive" matches the general policy.
items.commonMistake: Past or "would receive" suggests a hypothetical, not a regular procedure.
items.learningObjective: Company policies often use present + should.

items.question: Visitor badges _____ at the front desk on arrival.
items.explanation: Badges receive the action as a regular procedure: are issued.
items.commonMistake: "Issue" would need a subject who issues them. The badges are not doing the issuing.
items.learningObjective: Routine processes often appear as present passive.

items.question: Bonus payments _____ into staff accounts on the last Friday of March.
items.explanation: Payments are the object of the action. Future passive: will be deposited.
items.commonMistake: "Will deposit" is active and needs a depositor as subject.
items.learningObjective: Future passive = will be + past participle.

items.question: The minutes of Tuesday's planning session _____ on the shared drive.
items.explanation: The minutes received the action, and the result matters now: have been posted.
items.commonMistake: "Have posted" is active; minutes do not post themselves.
items.learningObjective: Present perfect passive = have/has been + past participle.

items.question: The afternoon train is _____ than the morning express, but it has more seats.
items.explanation: A comparison of two things uses the comparative: slower than.
items.commonMistake: "Slowest" is superlative (three or more). "Slow" needs the -er when than is present.
items.learningObjective: Look for than — that cue almost always means a comparative.

items.question: This year's catalog is not _____ colorful as the holiday edition.
items.explanation: The structure is as + adjective + as. "Not as colorful as" is the full pattern.
items.commonMistake: "More colorful as" mixes comparative and equative forms. Use more … than, or as … as.
items.learningObjective: Equality (or its negative) uses as + adj + as.

items.question: The revised budget includes _____ travel days than last quarter's plan.
items.explanation: "Days" is countable, so "fewer" is the correct comparative.
items.commonMistake: "Less" is for uncountable nouns (less time, less money). Travel days can be counted.
items.learningObjective: Fewer + countable plural; less + uncountable.

items.question: We look forward to _____ you at the product showcase next month.
items.explanation: In "look forward to," to is a preposition, so a gerund follows: meeting.
items.commonMistake: Learners treat to as an infinitive marker and choose "meet." Here to is not the infinitive.
items.learningObjective: After a preposition (including to in look forward to), use verb-ing.

items.question: The committee decided _____ the internship program for another year.
items.explanation: Decide is followed by a to-infinitive: decided to continue.
items.commonMistake: Decide + gerund is not standard. "Continue" without to is missing the infinitive marker.
items.learningObjective: Decide / hope / plan / expect + to + verb.

items.question: Please avoid _____ large files as attachments; use the shared folder instead.
items.explanation: Avoid is followed by a gerund: avoid sending.
items.commonMistake: Avoid to send is a frequent error. After avoid, enjoy, finish, keep — use -ing.
items.learningObjective: Avoid + verb-ing.

items.question: Please take _____ elevator on the left to reach the executive suite.
items.explanation: A specific elevator is identified ("on the left"), so "the" is required.
items.commonMistake: "A elevator" is also wrong because elevator begins with a vowel sound; but the real issue is specificity.
items.learningObjective: Use the when the listener can identify which one.

items.question: The firm is seeking _____ experienced auditor to join the internal review team.
items.explanation: "Experienced" begins with a vowel sound, so the indefinite article is "an."
items.commonMistake: "A experienced" breaks the a/an sound rule. "The" would point to a known person.
items.learningObjective: Choose a/an by the next sound, not the next letter.

items.question: There was _____ delay at customs, so the samples reached the showroom late.
items.explanation: "Delay" is a singular countable noun mentioned for the first time, so "a delay."
items.commonMistake: "An delay" fails the consonant-sound rule. "The delay" would refer to a delay already known.
items.learningObjective: First mention of a singular countable noun usually takes a/an.

items.question: Please leave the signed forms with _____ receptionist before you go upstairs.
items.explanation: In a workplace, "the receptionist" is a unique, known role at that site.
items.commonMistake: "A receptionist" would mean any receptionist, which is less natural for this building's desk.
items.learningObjective: Unique workplace roles often take the.

items.question: Employees _____ notify their supervisor if they will miss a scheduled shift.
items.explanation: "Should" gives a recommended workplace rule or duty.
items.commonMistake: "Would" is for hypotheticals. "Might have" refers to a past possibility, not a standing rule.
items.learningObjective: Should = advice or expected action in policies.

items.question: Visitors _____ enter the server room without an escort from IT.
items.explanation: "Must not" forbids an action. The rule bans unescorted entry.
items.commonMistake: "Need" requires "to" and does not by itself mean prohibition. "Ought" needs "to" as well.
items.learningObjective: Must not = it is not allowed.

items.question: The new packaging _____ reduce shipping damage, but we need more test data.
items.explanation: "Could" expresses a possible future benefit that is not yet proven.
items.commonMistake: "Must have" and "should have" talk about the past. "Used to" is a discontinued past habit.
items.learningObjective: Could + base verb = possible, not certain.

items.question: Several guests _____ to change their dinner reservation to 7:30.
items.explanation: "Would like to" is the polite request/wish pattern: would like + to-infinitive.
items.commonMistake: "Should have liked" is a past regret form and does not fit a current request.
items.learningObjective: Polite preference: would like to + verb.

items.question: The warehouse supervisor asked for a written _____ of each delayed shipment.
items.explanation: After "a written," a noun is required. "Explanation" names the document requested.
items.commonMistake: "Explanatory" is an adjective; "explain" is a verb.
items.learningObjective: Choose a noun when a determiner and adjective precede the blank.

items.question: The technician _____ restored network access for the accounting floor.
items.explanation: An adverb modifies the verb "restored." "Quickly" fits that role.
items.commonMistake: "Quick" is an adjective and does not modify a verb.
items.learningObjective: Use an adverb to describe how an action was performed.

items.question: After the product launch, client feedback was surprisingly _____.
items.explanation: After the linking verb "was," an adjective describes the subject. "Favorable" is correct.
items.commonMistake: "Favorably" is an adverb and does not follow a linking verb as a subject complement.
items.learningObjective: After be/seem/appear, choose an adjective, not an adverb.

items.question: The audit committee issued a _____ report recommending tighter expense controls.
items.explanation: The blank modifies "report," so an adjective is needed. "Conclusive" means decisive or definitive.
items.commonMistake: "Conclusion" is a noun; "conclusively" is an adverb.
items.learningObjective: Match word form to the slot: adjective before noun.

items.question: Ms. Okonkwo's _____ of the mentoring guidelines impressed the training board.
items.explanation: A possessive ("Ms. Okonkwo's") is followed by a noun. "Revision" is the noun form.
items.commonMistake: "Revise" is a verb; gerunds are less natural after a person's possessive naming a finished product.
items.learningObjective: After a possessive, prefer a noun naming the product or action.

items.question: The help desk _____ ticket volume since the software upgrade began last week.
items.explanation: "Since" plus a continuing action calls for present perfect continuous: "has been monitoring."
items.commonMistake: Simple past "monitored" does not show an action still ongoing from a past starting point.
items.learningObjective: Use present perfect continuous with since/for for actions that started in the past and continue.

items.question: By the time the shuttle arrived, most passengers _____ already checked in online.
items.explanation: Past perfect "had … checked" places the online check-in before another past event (the shuttle's arrival).
items.commonMistake: "Have" is present perfect and does not fit a clearly finished past sequence.
items.learningObjective: Use past perfect for the earlier of two past actions.

items.question: Facilities _____ the fourth-floor carpets this week, so some desks are temporarily relocated.
items.explanation: "This week" with an unfinished workplace project fits present continuous "are replacing."
items.commonMistake: Simple present "replace" suggests a habitual action, not a temporary project.
items.learningObjective: Use present continuous for temporary actions happening around now.

items.question: According to the agenda, Mr. Chen _____ introduce the new vendors after lunch.
items.explanation: A planned future action on an agenda uses "is going to" + base verb.
items.commonMistake: "Goes to" is present simple and does not mark a planned future introduction.
items.learningObjective: Use be going to for planned future actions.

items.question: Our agents _____ already processed most of this morning's refund requests.
items.explanation: Plural subject "agents" + "already" + past participle needs "have" (present perfect).
items.commonMistake: "Has" agrees with a singular subject, not "agents."
items.learningObjective: Pair present perfect with already/yet for completed recent actions.

items.question: Distribution centers rely _____ accurate tracking data to schedule outbound trucks.
items.explanation: The collocation is "rely on" someone or something.
items.commonMistake: "Rely in" and "rely at" are not standard English collocations.
items.learningObjective: Memorize verb + preposition pairs such as rely on.

items.question: Ms. Rivera is in charge _____ booking conference rooms for visiting clients.
items.explanation: The fixed phrase is "in charge of" + gerund/noun.
items.commonMistake: "In charge to" confuses this phrase with "responsible to" (a person).
items.learningObjective: Use of after in charge when naming a duty.

items.question: _____ the latest forecast, operating costs will decline slightly in Q4.
items.explanation: "According to" introduces a source of information.
items.commonMistake: "According with" is incorrect; use "in accordance with" for rules/compliance.
items.learningObjective: Use according to before a report, person, or data source.

items.question: Staff should be aware _____ the planned outage before opening support tickets.
items.explanation: The adjective phrase is "aware of" + noun.
items.commonMistake: "Aware to" is not idiomatic; "aware of" is the standard collocation.
items.learningObjective: Link aware with of when naming knowledge or a fact.

items.question: The proposal was well researched; _____, the board postponed a final vote.
items.explanation: The second clause contrasts with the first, so "however" is the right transition.
items.commonMistake: "Therefore" signals result, not contrast.
items.learningObjective: Use however to mark unexpected contrast between clauses.

items.question: Delivery routes were redrawn _____ several bridges were closed for repairs.
items.explanation: "Because" introduces the reason the routes were redrawn.
items.commonMistake: "Although" would reverse the logic into contrast rather than cause.
items.learningObjective: Choose because for cause-effect between clauses.

items.question: New hires receive laptop setup on day one; _____, they attend a benefits briefing.
items.explanation: "In addition" adds a second onboarding step to the first.
items.commonMistake: "Instead" replaces one action with another; both actions occur here.
items.learningObjective: Use in addition to stack related workplace actions.

items.question: Agents save call notes carefully _____ supervisors can review unresolved cases later.
items.explanation: "So that" introduces purpose: notes are saved to enable later review.
items.commonMistake: "Even if" introduces a concessive condition, not purpose.
items.learningObjective: Use so that to show purpose between two clauses.

items.question: Please contact the representative _____ territory includes the western districts.
items.explanation: "Whose" shows possession linking the representative to "territory."
items.commonMistake: "Who" cannot mark possession before a noun like "territory."
items.learningObjective: Use whose for possessive relative clauses about people.

items.question: The receptionist asked _____ to wait in the lobby until a badge was ready.
items.explanation: After the verb "asked," an object pronoun is required: "us."
items.commonMistake: "We" is a subject pronoun and cannot be the object of asked.
items.learningObjective: Use object pronouns after verbs and prepositions.

items.question: Mr. Haddad reserved the hotel room _____, without using the travel desk.
items.explanation: A reflexive pronoun is needed when the subject and object are the same person: "himself."
items.commonMistake: "Him" would imply a different person reserved the room for Mr. Haddad.
items.learningObjective: Use reflexive pronouns for actions done by the subject to/for the subject.

items.question: The patch _____ fixed the login error was installed overnight.
items.explanation: "Which" refers to a thing ("the patch") in a relative clause.
items.commonMistake: "Who" is reserved for people, not software patches.
items.learningObjective: Use which (or that) for relative clauses about things.

items.question: Each of the applicants _____ required to submit a writing sample.
items.explanation: "Each" is singular, so the verb is "is" even though "applicants" is plural.
items.commonMistake: Agreeing with "applicants" instead of with "each."
items.learningObjective: Treat each/every as singular subjects.

items.question: The number of overdue invoices _____ decreased since reminders were automated.
items.explanation: "The number of" takes a singular verb: "has decreased."
items.commonMistake: Confusing "the number of" (singular) with "a number of" (plural).
items.learningObjective: Use a singular verb after the number of + plural noun.

items.question: Either the drivers or the dispatcher _____ the load sheets before departure.
items.explanation: With either…or, the verb agrees with the nearer subject "dispatcher" (singular): "signs."
items.commonMistake: Agreeing with "drivers" instead of the subject closest to the verb.
items.learningObjective: In either…or / neither…nor, agree with the nearest noun.

items.question: The marketing firm _____ several campaigns for regional retailers each spring.
items.explanation: In American workplace English, a company/firm as a unit takes a singular verb: "designs."
items.commonMistake: Using plural "design" as if "firm" were plural.
items.learningObjective: Treat company/organization names as singular in formal US English.

items.question: If the auditor finishes early, we _____ start the exit interview before noon.
items.explanation: A real future possibility after present-tense if uses "will" in the result clause.
items.commonMistake: "Would" belongs in second-conditional (unreal present) patterns.
items.learningObjective: First conditional: if + present, will + base verb.

items.question: If the printer _____ working, staff would not need to walk to another floor.
items.explanation: Second conditional uses past form in the if-clause; "were" is standard for unreal present.
items.commonMistake: Using present "is" would make a first conditional, which needs "will" not "would."
items.learningObjective: Second conditional: if + past, would + base verb.

items.question: If the visas _____ been approved sooner, the engineers would have joined the site visit.
items.explanation: Third conditional uses "had" + past participle in the if-clause for unreal past.
items.commonMistake: "Have been" is present perfect and does not form the unreal past.
items.learningObjective: Third conditional: if + had + PP, would have + PP.

items.question: Refunds will not be issued _____ customers return the unused product within 14 days.
items.explanation: "Unless" means "if not": no refund without a timely return.
items.commonMistake: "If" would reverse the intended meaning (refunds when they return).
items.learningObjective: Use unless for negative conditions in policies.

items.question: Last week's safety briefing _____ by the regional operations director.
items.explanation: The briefing is the object of the action; "was led" is past simple passive.
items.commonMistake: Active "led" would need a subject who did the leading, not "by" alone.
items.learningObjective: Use was/were + past participle for finished past passives.

items.question: All passwords _____ be reset after a suspected security breach.
items.explanation: Modal + passive = modal + be + past participle. With "be reset" already in the sentence, choose "must."
items.commonMistake: "Must be" would duplicate "be" already present after the blank.
items.learningObjective: Form modal passives with modal + be + past participle; watch words already in the stem.

items.question: New ID badges _____ printed in the security office this afternoon.
items.explanation: Present continuous passive is "are being" + past participle for an action in progress.
items.commonMistake: "Are printed" is present simple passive and misses the ongoing sense of "this afternoon."
items.learningObjective: Use am/is/are being + PP for passive actions happening now.

items.question: Damaged crates _____ inspected before they are returned to the supplier.
items.explanation: Advice in the passive uses "should be" + past participle.
items.commonMistake: "Should inspected" omits the required be before the past participle.
items.learningObjective: Combine modals of advice with be + PP for passive recommendations.

items.question: This brochure is _____ detailed than the one distributed last season.
items.explanation: Comparative with than uses "more" + adjective for longer adjectives like "detailed."
items.commonMistake: "Most" forms a superlative and does not pair with than for two items.
items.learningObjective: Use more + adj + than for longer adjectives.

items.question: Among the three vendors, Apex offered the _____ competitive annual fee.
items.explanation: Comparing three vendors requires the superlative "the most competitive."
items.commonMistake: "More" is for comparing only two things.
items.learningObjective: Use the most + adj when ranking three or more options.

items.question: Please schedule _____ meetings this month so teams can finish project work.
items.explanation: "Meetings" is countable, so "fewer" is preferred over "less."
items.commonMistake: Using "less" with countable plural nouns in formal English.
items.learningObjective: Prefer fewer with countable plurals; less with uncountables.

items.question: The _____ agents respond to chats, the higher customer satisfaction scores rise.
items.explanation: The correlative pattern "the + comparative, the + comparative" needs "faster."
items.commonMistake: Superlative "fastest" does not fit the the…the structure.
items.learningObjective: Recognize the + comparative … the + comparative patterns.

items.question: Managers suggested _____ the wellness survey before the holiday break.
items.explanation: "Suggest" is followed by a gerund: "suggested distributing."
items.commonMistake: "Suggest to distribute" mirrors other verbs incorrectly; suggest takes -ing.
items.learningObjective: After suggest/recommend/avoid, use a gerund.

items.question: The sales team plans _____ three regional offices next quarter.
items.explanation: "Plan" takes a to-infinitive: "plans to visit."
items.commonMistake: "Plan visiting" is nonstandard; use to + base verb.
items.learningObjective: After plan/hope/agree/decide, use to-infinitive.

items.question: New interns are not yet used to _____ in an open-plan workspace.
items.explanation: "Be used to" means accustomed to and is followed by a gerund or noun.
items.commonMistake: Confusing "be used to + -ing" with "used to + base verb" (past habit).
items.learningObjective: After be/get used to, use a gerund.

items.question: Please do not forget _____ the conference call details to the client tonight.
items.explanation: "Forget to" + infinitive means fail to do a required future/present action.
items.commonMistake: "Forget sending" refers to not remembering a past action, not a reminder.
items.learningObjective: Forget/remember + to-infinitive = (not) doing a duty.

items.question: _____ employees must complete the ethics module before accessing client files.
items.explanation: General plural nouns often take no article: "Employees must…"
items.commonMistake: Adding "The" when the sentence refers to employees in general, not a specific group already identified.
items.learningObjective: Omit articles before general plural countable nouns.

items.question: Do we have _____ spare HDMI cables in the AV closet?
items.explanation: Questions about existence usually use "any" with plural/uncountable nouns.
items.commonMistake: "Some" is more common in offers/requests than in neutral yes/no existence questions.
items.learningObjective: Prefer any in most questions and negatives with plural nouns.

items.question: If this pallet is damaged, please request _____ one from the staging area.
items.explanation: "Another" means one additional singular countable item: "another one."
items.commonMistake: "Other" needs a plural noun or "the other" for a specific remaining item.
items.learningObjective: Use another before singular countable nouns.

items.question: Please book _____ earliest flight that arrives before the afternoon workshop.
items.explanation: Superlatives take "the": "the earliest flight."
items.commonMistake: Omitting the article before a superlative adjective + noun.
items.learningObjective: Always use the before superlative forms.

items.question: Accountants _____ to attach receipts when they submit mileage claims.
items.explanation: "Have to" expresses external obligation; the blank needs "have" before "to attach."
items.commonMistake: "Must to" is ungrammatical; must is followed by a bare infinitive.
items.learningObjective: Recognize have to as a modal-like obligation form.

items.question: Restarting the router _____ resolve the intermittent connection drops.
items.explanation: "Might" + base verb expresses possibility without certainty.
items.commonMistake: "Ought" requires "to" (ought to); alone it is incomplete.
items.learningObjective: Use might/may + base verb for uncertain outcomes.

items.question: The team _____ have confirmed the dial-in code before inviting external guests.
items.explanation: "Should have" + past participle criticizes a past action that was advisable but not done.
items.commonMistake: "Must have" expresses deduction about the past, not regretful advice.
items.learningObjective: Use should have + PP for past advice/criticism.

items.question: Callers _____ not remain on hold if they prefer a callback within one hour.
items.explanation: "Need not" means it is not necessary to stay on hold.
items.commonMistake: "Must not" means prohibition, which is stronger and wrong here.
items.learningObjective: Distinguish need not (no necessity) from must not (prohibition).
